paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: you can bring the LORD your honest cry, even the "be not deaf to me" kind (Psalm 28:1). David doesn't polish his prayer. He says out loud that God's silence feels like life or death, and he lifts his hands and asks for mercy (Psalm 28:2). I spent years in a drawer wondering if anybody was listening, so hear me: God wants the real prayer, not the pretty one.

Now watch what happens in the middle. David asks the LORD not to drag him away with people who "speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts" (Psalm 28:3). Then he says the LORD will tear down those who show no regard for what His hands have done (Psalm 28:5). I think the lesson is that you can ask God to keep you from the two-faced life, and you can leave the settling up to Him. That's not your job, baker, and thank goodness, because my arms are a mustache.

Then the psalm turns: "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy." (Psalm 28:6) David says, "The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped." (Psalm 28:7) He doesn't stay in the worry, and he doesn't keep it to himself. He ends by asking the LORD to "shepherd them and carry them forever." (Psalm 28:9) So when you pray, friend, bring Him the cry, trust Him with the answer, and sing when you're helped.
